title: 487. Sets, Logic, Reasoning & Proof: Negation of Propositions
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Write the negation of a strict inequality.
questions.question: For a real number \(x\), what is the negation of the statement \(x>3\)?
questions.explanation: The negation must be true exactly when \(x>3\) is false. If \(x\) is not greater than \(3\), then \(x\) is less than or equal to \(3\). The statement \(x<3\) is not the negation, because for \(x=3\) both \(x>3\) and \(x<3\) are false.
questions.hint: Test the value \(x=3\): exactly one of a statement and its negation must be true.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of the negation of a true proposition.
questions.question: The proposition \(p\) is true. What is the truth value of \(\neg p\)?
questions.explanation: The negation \(\neg p\) has the opposite truth value of \(p\). Since \(p\) is true, \(\neg p\) is false.
questions.hint: A proposition and its negation never have the same truth value.

questions.learningObjective: Write the negation of an equation.
questions.question: What is the negation of the statement \(x=5\)?
questions.explanation: The negation of "\(x\) equals \(5\)" is "\(x\) does not equal \(5\)", written \(x\ne 5\). The statement \(x=-5\) is just another specific equation; for \(x=0\) both \(x=5\) and \(x=-5\) are false, so it is not the negation.
questions.hint: The negation must be true for every value of \(x\) that makes the original false.

questions.concept: Negation of a true arithmetic statement
questions.learningObjective: Determine the truth value of the negation of a true statement.
questions.question: What is the truth value of the negation of the statement "\(2+2=4\)"?
questions.explanation: The statement "\(2+2=4\)" is true. Its negation, "\(2+2\ne 4\)", therefore has the opposite truth value and is false.
questions.hint: First decide whether the original statement is true.

questions.learningObjective: Write the negation of a non-strict inequality.
questions.question: For real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), what is the negation of the statement \(a\le b\)?
questions.explanation: If \(a\) is not less than or equal to \(b\), then \(a\) is greater than \(b\). So the negation is \(a>b\). The statement \(a\ge b\) is not the negation: when \(a=b\), both \(a\le b\) and \(a\ge b\) are true.
questions.hint: Test the case \(a=b\): a statement and its negation cannot both be true.

questions.learningObjective: Write the negation of a statement about the parity of an integer.
questions.question: For an integer \(n\), what is the negation of the statement "\(n\) is even"?
questions.explanation: Every integer is either even or odd, and never both. So "\(n\) is not even" means exactly "\(n\) is odd". The statement "\(-n\) is even" is equivalent to the original statement, not its negation, because \(n\) and \(-n\) have the same parity.
questions.hint: The negation must be true exactly when the original statement is false.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the negation of a statement from a different, more specific statement.
questions.question: What is the negation of the statement "The triangle is isosceles"?
questions.explanation: The negation simply denies the statement: the triangle is not isosceles, meaning that no two of its sides are equal. The statement "The triangle is equilateral" is not the negation; an equilateral triangle has at least two equal sides, so it is itself isosceles.
questions.hint: A negation must be false whenever the original statement is true.

questions.learningObjective: Write the negation of a positivity statement without forgetting zero.
questions.question: For a real number \(x\), what is the negation of the statement "\(x\) is positive"?
questions.explanation: "\(x\) is positive" means \(x>0\). Its negation is \(x\le 0\): the number is negative or zero. The statement \(x<0\) leaves out zero; for \(x=0\) both "\(x\) is positive" and "\(x\) is negative" are false, so "negative" is not the negation of "positive".
questions.hint: Consider the value \(x=0\), which is neither positive nor negative.

questions.concept: A false proposition and its negation
questions.learningObjective: Assign truth values to a false proposition and to its negation.
questions.question: Let \(p\) be the proposition "\(\sqrt{2}\) is a rational number". Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: \(p\) is false and \(\neg p\) is true.

questions.explanation: The number \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational, so \(p\) is false. Its negation \(\neg p\), "\(\sqrt{2}\) is not a rational number", is therefore true. A proposition and its negation always have opposite truth values, so they can never both be false.
questions.hint: Decide the truth value of \(p\); the negation must have the opposite value.
